The polls are open. Day two of early voting runs 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. today across Webb County's 14 early-voting locations, and voters in Laredo are choosing the next mayor, four city council seats, a municipal court judge, and — in the congressional race — Texas's 28th District representative.

One figure is conspicuously missing from this picture: how many people voted on day one.

As of this morning, the Webb County Elections Office had not published cumulative turnout figures for Monday's first day of early voting — no in-person count, no mail-ballot tally, no running total. That's the number that tells voters whether the county's early-voting engine is humming or sputtering, and it isn't public yet.

What we know, and what we don't

Here's what's verified, according to the county's published schedules, the Texas Secretary of State, and local reporting:

  • Hours this week: 8 a.m.–6 p.m. Monday–Friday (Oct. 19–23); Saturday Oct. 24, 8 a.m.–8 p.m.; Sunday Oct. 25, 12 p.m.–6 p.m.; Monday–Friday Oct. 26–30, 8 a.m.–8 p.m.
  • Locations: 14 early-voting sites countywide. The main site is the Webb County Elections Office, 720 Convent Ave. in Laredo. Branch locations include the Barbara Fasken Recreation Center, the Laredo Fire Department Administrative Center, the City Hall Annex, and the McKendrick/Ochoa/Salinas Library, plus nine temporary branches countywide.
  • Mail ballots: Applications for a ballot by mail must be received by the county by Friday, October 23. A postmark alone doesn't satisfy the deadline, according to the Secretary of State.
  • Election Day: Tuesday, November 3, 7 a.m.–7 p.m. Webb County uses countywide vote centers — voters may use any of 39 locations, not just their home precinct.

What's on the ballot: Mayor — incumbent Dr. Victor Treviño faces JD Gonzalez, Alfonso "Poncho" Casso, Alyssa Cigarroa, and Jorge A. Garza — plus city council Districts I, II, III, and VI, Municipal Court Judge Place 1, and the Cuellar–Tijerina contest for Congress in TX-28.

The turnout question nobody has answered yet

Turnout in Laredo's municipal elections has historically been low — often well below half of registered voters — and early voting is where most of those votes are cast. In the March primary earlier this year, Webb County Elections Administrator José Luis Castillo projected overall turnout of roughly 30 to 35 percent, according to KGNS reporting, while noting that the county's participation has run above the state average in recent years. The county had roughly 147,000 registered voters at that time, per KGNS.

Statewide, Secretary of State Robert S. Howden announced a record of more than 19 million registered Texans for this election, and urged voters to rely on official information at VoteTexas.gov.

But none of that tells us how day one went in Webb County. Did lines form at the Convent Avenue office Monday morning? Did the machines behave? Did any precinct report staffing problems? As of publication, no local outlet — and no official county channel we could verify — has reported the first day's numbers or flagged any problems.

The day-one story that wasn't about turnout

The one piece of election news that did break Monday concerned the sheriff's race's shadow, not the ballot box. Gov. Greg Abbott's campaign opened early voting by announcing endorsements from Democratic border-county sheriffs — a list that initially included Webb County Sheriff Martin Cuellar, who is under federal indictment. By late Monday morning, Cuellar's name had been quietly removed from the campaign's list with no explanation, according to Texas Gazette reporting. Sheriff Cuellar has not been convicted of any crime, and the indictment's allegations remain unproven.

The watchdog's questions for the county, now that day two is underway:

  1. Release day-one figures — today. Counties across Texas routinely publish daily in-person and mail-ballot totals during early voting. Webb County voters deserve a running count, starting with Monday's.
  2. Say how it compares. Raw numbers mean little without context. Is day one on pace with — or behind — comparable elections?
  3. Report problems promptly. If lines, equipment, or staffing hiccups happened Monday, voters have a right to know before they show up today.

The absence of a reported problem is not proof there wasn't one. And the absence of numbers is itself a data point — it tells you what the county is choosing to share.

Early voting continues through Friday, October 30. We'll be watching the totals — as soon as the county publishes them.

excerpt: Early voting's second day opens in Webb County with no first-day turnout figures released. Here's what's open, what's at stake, and what the county should be telling voters.
title: Early Voting Day Two: Laredo Polls Open at 8, but Webb County Hasn't Released First-Day Turnout
